text: PASSAGE (SRC-03-P1): The story of Eklavya is usually told as a lesson in devotion. A tribal boy, refused instruction by the royal teacher Drona, makes a clay image of the master and practises before it until his archery rivals that of the finest prince. When Drona learns of this, he asks for his fee: the boy's right thumb. Eklavya gives it without a murmur, and the tale praises his obedience. Yet many modern readers find the same episode troubling for a different reason. It shows talent that grew without privilege being deliberately cut short so that a favoured pupil might remain unrivalled. Read this way, the story is less about loyalty than about the gatekeeping of skill, and about how institutions can protect rank by denying opportunity. Neither reading is entirely wrong. The epic does not hide the injustice; it records it plainly and leaves the listener uneasy. Perhaps that is its lasting value. A story that only rewarded virtue might be forgotten quickly, but one that makes us ask whether merit was truly honoured keeps returning, generation after generation, as a question rather than an answer. || What is the central theme of the passage?

option_D: Eklavya was the greatest archer of the epic age

text: PASSAGE (SRC-03-P2): Automated systems now help to approve loans, sort job applications and flag suspicious transactions. Their appeal is easy to understand: they work quickly, never tire and apply the same rule to every case. Yet these strengths conceal a weakness. A system trained on past decisions can absorb the biases of those decisions and repeat them at a scale no single clerk could reach. Because its reasoning is often hidden inside layers of calculation, an unfair outcome may go unnoticed for months. For this reason, many experts argue that important decisions should keep a person 'in the loop', someone who can question an output, ask for an explanation and overrule the machine when needed. Oversight of this kind is not a sign of distrust in technology, any more than a co-pilot is a sign of distrust in the pilot. It does, however, carry costs. A reviewer who checks thousands of cases may begin to approve whatever the system suggests, turning supervision into a mere formality. Effective oversight therefore depends on giving reviewers time, training and genuine authority, so that the human check remains a real judgement rather than a signature. || According to the passage, an unfair outcome produced by an automated system may go unnoticed because:

A system trained on past decisions can absorb the biases of those decisions and repeat them at a scale no single clerk could reach. Because its reasoning is often hidden inside layers of calculation, an unfair outcome may go unnoticed for months. For this reason, many experts argue that important decisions should keep a person 'in the loop', someone who can question an output, ask for an explanation and overrule the machine when needed. Oversight of this kind is not a sign of distrust in technology, any more than a co-pilot is a sign of distrust in the pilot. It does, however, carry costs. A reviewer who checks thousands of cases may begin to approve whatever the system suggests, turning supervision into a mere formality. Effective oversight therefore depends on giving reviewers time, training and genuine authority, so that the human check remains a real judgement rather than a signature. || What is the central theme of the passage?
option_A: Machines should replace clerks in every office
option_B: Automated systems are always biased and should be banned
option_C: Training reviewers is the costliest part of any business
option_D: Automated decision systems are useful but need meaningful human oversight, which must itself be properly supported

text: PASSAGE (SRC-03-P3): In many parts of India a length of handwoven cloth can tell an observer where it was made. The motifs, the colours favoured and even the way the border meets the body of the fabric carry the memory of a region, passed from one generation of weavers to the next. For this reason, handloom is often defended not merely as a craft but as a living record of local identity. The difficulty is that identity alone does not pay the weaver. A sari that takes three weeks on a loom must compete with machine-made copies that imitate its pattern at a fraction of the price, and many young people from weaving families now prefer steadier work in towns. Some efforts to help have backfired, encouraging weavers to change traditional designs so completely to suit distant buyers that the cloth loses the very distinctiveness that made it valuable. More durable answers seem to combine respect for tradition with practical support: protected names for regional products, fair access to markets and design advice that adapts colours or uses without erasing the core motifs. A tradition, after all, survives only if those who carry it can also make a living from it. || Which of the following is the closest synonym of the word 'durable' as used in the passage?
